content: Canada balsam, also known as Canada turpentine or balsam of fir, is a turpentine derived from the resin of the balsam fir tree (Abies balsamea). This resin is dissolved in essential oils, resulting in a viscous, sticky, and colorless (or occasionally yellowish) liquid. When the essential oils evaporate, the substance solidifies into a transparent yellowish mass. Canada balsam is highly valued for its exceptional optical properties. It has a refractive index of approximately 1.55, which is very close to that of glass, making it an ideal adhesive for optical applications. Its purity and stability are notable, as it does not crystallize with age, ensuring that its optical properties remain consistent over time. Additionally, it is soluble in xylene and forms an amorphous solid when dried. In biological applications, Canada balsam is used to preserve microscopic samples. It acts as an adhesive to secure a sample between a microscope slide and a coverslip, effectively enclosing and conserving the specimen. In optical technology, Canada balsam is employed to bond optical components, such as joining two prisms to create a beam splitter or adhering two lenses together. Canada balsam is also used to repair scratches in glass, such as car windshields, in a manner that minimizes visibility. Furthermore, in oil painting, it is utilized to enhance the luminosity of the artwork and to facilitate the blending of colors. It is important to note that Canada balsam is sometimes mistakenly referred to as Balm of Gilead. However, the true balsam is derived from a fir tree, whereas Balm of Gilead originates from a type of poplar tree.
